• Scientific name: Staurogyne repens
  • Other names: Mud mat
  • Tank size (minimum): 10 gallons (~40 liters)
  • Difficulty: Easy to medium
  • Lighting: Medium to high
  • Optimal pH: 6.0 – 7.0
  • Optimal GH: 1 – 10
  • Optimal temperature: 22 – 30 °C (72 – 86 °F)
  • Substrate: Needed (nutrient-rich)
  • Growth rate: Slow
  • Placement in tank: Mostly foreground / midground
  • Height: 8 – 10 cm (up to 4 inches)
  • Fertilizer: Recommended
  • CO2: Not needed – low
  • Propagation: By side shoots and vegetative buds

Staurogyne repens is a versatile aquarium plant that belongs to Acanthaceae, a family of dicotyledonous floating plants with about 250 genera and over 2500 species.

The genus Staurogyne contains six freshwater species and the most common is Staurogyne repens, which is famous for its use in decorating freshwater aquariums.

This freshwater plant species originates from the Rio Cristalino in Mato Grosso in the South Amazonas. There, the small plant grows on and between hardscapes (rocks) on the shores of the fast-flowing river.

Interesting fact: Staurogyne repens also has a food value. This plant grows wild and native people often cook rice with its leaves to give a pleasant taste to the rice.

Staurogyne repens should be planted in a freshwater tank of at least 10 gallons (~40 liters). This tank size ensures that the plant has sufficient room, especially when horizontal shoots start to spread.

There isn't much to do when it comes to taking care of this hardy plant; its size and slow growth habit make maintenance easy.

Since the plant is not a fast grower, you won't have to trim the shoots all the time. If the carpet gets high or you notice areas with considerably more height than others, do a quick trim to keep the carpet level, neat and compact.

Note: Although everybody mentions Staurogyne repens as a carpet plant, technically it is not. Staurogyne repens is a stem plant that does not carpet. However, we can get the carpet effect by trimming and replanting the cuttings.

You can also use this opportunity to clip decaying leaves and stems; the aim is to remove the browns from the greens to achieve a uniform and attractive carpet.

Make sure to perform regular water changes to keep the water pristine and clear. Clear water helps light penetrate to the plants at the lower levels, which include your Staurogyne carpet.

To ensure that the plants get essential nutrients in abundance, dose liquid supplements in the right amounts into the tank water. This encourages healthy growth and development of the roots and shoots; if you want to maintain a fresh, dense, and bright green carpet, integrate this practice into your maintenance regime.

Temperature: The ideal temperature range for growing Staurogyne repens is 20 – 30 °C (68 – 86 °F); best growth is attained in tanks with warm water.

pH: Even though Staurogyne repens can tolerate a huge range of pH (from 5.0 to 8.0), the optimal pH is 6.0 – 7.0.

Hardness: The plant appreciates soft to moderately hard water with ideal values between 1 – 10 dGH.

Lighting

Staurogyne repens needs bright illumination to thrive in the aquarium, so medium to high lighting should be supplied (30 – 50 PAR). Under low lighting, the plant starts growing upwards as if trying to reach the surface for better light.

Maintain a photoperiod of up to 10 hours daily; keeping the lights on longer will trigger the growth of unwanted algae. A full spectrum LED lighting fixture can be used to provide the required light intensity.

Substrate

The plant prefers a nutrient-rich substrate, such as a mixture of small-sized gravel and aquarium soil, or aquarium soil alone.

Fine-grained aquarium substrates allow the tiny roots of Staurogyne repens to penetrate easily and provide better anchorage. Some recommended substrates for this plant include:

  • ADA Amazonia aqua soil,
  • Carib Sea Eco-Complete,
  • Seachem Fluorite.

These substrates are rich in nutrients and also allow the thin roots of Staurogyne repens to penetrate easily.

CO2 and fertilization

This species can thrive without CO2, so it can be planted in low-tech tanks. However, adding CO2 and liquid fertilizers is quite beneficial as it makes ample nutrients readily accessible to the plants, preventing nutrient deficiency and poor health, and accelerating growth and overall development.

Even though Staurogyne repens has a large root system, the plant still feeds from both the water column and the roots. So, besides using root tabs, make it a habit to dose liquid fertilizers in the water column from time to time, plus CO2 — using either liquid CO2 or a pressurized CO2 system.

Important: If you keep shrimp in the tank with Staurogyne repens, note that a high level of CO2 and copper (most fertilizers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

The delicate and palatable nature of Staurogyne repens makes it picky about suitable tankmates. The plant will survive in tanks with animals that won't see its soft leaves as a snack. Compatible tankmates include:

Fish: Staurogyne repens is best kept with small, peaceful community fish such as bleeding heart tetra, neon tetras, mollies, killifish, swordtails, White Mountain minnows, zebra danio, sunburst platy, Endlers, Otocinclus catfish and pygmy Corydoras.

Shrimp: Since Staurogyne repens can tolerate a wide range of pH, it can be kept with any dwarf shrimp species.

Freshwater snails: Ornamental snails should not be kept in a tank with low pH for a long time, as it will negatively affect their shells. However, if your pH is close to 7.0, you can keep almost any snail or dwarf shrimp you like, for example Japanese trapdoor snails, ramshorn snails, nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, black devil snails, Asolene spixi, rabbit snails, etc.

Avoid

Avoid species that may find Staurogyne repens palatable, such as koi, goldfish, Oscars, rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey, clown loaches and African cichlids. These species can cause problems in planted tanks.

Staurogyne repens and most types of crayfish or freshwater crabs are also not a good combination. These animals will cut, eat, and uproot everything in the tank.

Planting

Planting Staurogyne repens is not difficult, but you should follow a specific planting guideline to achieve the right quantity and quality of foreground vegetation.

Some aquarists say to observe a planting rule of one stem for every 2 gallons (~8 L) in order to prevent overcrowding. Eventually, though, the stems will grow together into a thick mat.

In the beginning, it is better to keep a spacing of about 2 – 3 inches (5 – 7 cm) between stems. It reduces competition at the early stage and lets them establish.

Bury each stem about ½ – ¾ of an inch (about 1.5 – 2 cm) deep into the substrate. The thin roots will easily penetrate the substrate when planted this way. Individual plants can be placed into the substrate using tweezers.

Wait 3–4 weeks and check the growth; if there are large spaces that still need to be filled, add a few more stems.

Dose liquid fertilizers and keep trimming the shoots from time to time to encourage horizontal growth. If you have floating plants in the tank, make sure the water surface is clear enough to allow light to reach the carpet.

If done properly, the desired carpeting effect will be achieved after a few months.

Propagation

Staurogyne repens is capable of forming vegetative buds, and this habit is more common in its emergent form.

Side shoots tend to emerge from the parent plant; these parts detach and fall onto the soil, then grow and develop into individual plants. In the aquarium, you can simply clip mature stems and replant them in the substrate.

You do not need to take out the whole stem; just make a sizeable cutting of roughly 2 inches (5 cm) and place it into the substrate. Even without visible roots, the cutting will thrive and gradually develop into a new plant.

Alternative way of growing

If you are starting a new tank, you may use the dry start method: cultivate the stems in a nutrient-rich substrate, spray water regularly to provide humidity, then fill the tank with water when the plant's growth kicks off.

The dry start method significantly boosts the development of slow-growing plants, cycles the substrate, and removes algae problems.

Description

In appearance, Staurogyne repens is similar to and closely related to Hygrophila, which is also found in South American waters. The distinction between the two plant groups is that the leaves of Hygrophila are bigger and longer than those of Staurogyne repens, in addition to the difference in growth rate—known species of Hygrophila grow faster than Staurogyne repens.

Staurogyne repens has an overall bright green coloration with green or brown stems. The leaves are small and thin, typically oval and broad towards the base. The plant has a soft/smooth texture, which makes it an easy target for plant-eating fish and some snail species, so you ought to be careful when choosing tankmates.

Staurogyne repens develops horizontally creeping shoots from the base which tend to form a low and compact covering on the aquarium floor. The typical size of the carpet is about 4 inches (10 cm), earning the plant a spot as one of the best foreground plants for aquascaping.

Melting

This is a common phenomenon in plants during a transition from emersed to submersed form. When an emersed-grown Staurogyne repens is cultivated submersed in an aquarium, the initial leaves will melt/die off to make way for new leaves, and growth of the plant continues. As long as the stems are green, there is no need to worry too much; it will resprout.

Note: Sometimes Staurogyne repens can melt after months of thriving. Aquarists call it Staurogyne melt syndrome. Unfortunately, nobody really knows what causes it.

Discolored leaves

Yellow or faded leaves are often a sign of nutrient deficiency. To remedy this, boost the iron (Fe) content of the tank water by dosing enough chelated iron.

Likewise, make sure to provide sufficient macro and trace nutrients to support the active and healthy growth of this species. The availability of essential nutrients in the substrate and tank water, in addition to CO2, will help keep the leaves fresh and bright green.

Leggy growth

The aim of cultivating a low foreground plant is to achieve a nice, compact carpet in the front of the tank, but in some cases the plant tends to grow vertically towards the surface instead of horizontally.

The stronger the light intensity, the denser and more compact the carpet will be; when the carpet is grown in low light, it will look leggy and unattractive.

Buying

This species is readily available in local fish stores; if you don't find it at nearby stores, look online, as there are plenty of online vendors that stock this plant.

Avoid unhealthy or damaged plants, since they don't do well when cultivated in the tank. Typically, healthy stems are fresh, upright, with green or slight brown coloration. A sizeable bunch containing up to 10 stems should be enough to aquascape a 10–20 gallon fish tank.

Quarantine

Quarantine Staurogyne repens before putting it into your aquarium if necessary. For example, there is no need to do so if the plants are "in vitro", meaning they are cultivated on nutrient media under sterile laboratory conditions. In all other cases:

  • The plant can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly, damselfly nymphs, etc.).
  • It could also have been treated with chemicals (pesticide) to remove parasites, snails, etc. These chemicals are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp, and other invertebrates.

Note: According to a study, Staurogyne repens is hardy enough to tolerate a relatively high concentration of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). The best results were found in explants treated with 5.5% H2O2 for 20 minutes.

Conclusion

For a hardy plant that can form a beautiful and thick lawn on the bottom of the aquarium, Staurogyne repens is a good fit. It is slow-growing, thrives with or without CO2 and takes up to 2–3 months after planting to densely cover the foreground of the tank, so frequent trimming of the shoots is not needed.
